findings.text: Host second stage mapping granularity is forced to single pages except for two canonical cases. Memory ranges may use larger mappings only with the standard host memory protection, and other ranges may use larger mappings only with the standard host MMIO protection. All other protections use page mappings because the host table is the only record of that state and a later page scoped map could otherwise split a block and lose state that cannot be rebuilt on demand.

A range validation context stores a wanted page state together with a helper that derives the current state from a table entry and address. Its visitor calls the helper for the visited location and signals success when the derived state matches the wanted state, otherwise it signals a permission failure.

Operations that share or unshare a guest page with the host hold two component locks in a fixed order. The host lock is taken first, then the guest lock for the owning virtual machine, both are held across validation and table updates, and both are released on every path including early validation failure.

Guest initiated sharing acts on one page identified from a guest frame number. Sharing requires the guest entry to be owned and the host entry to be absent, then moves the guest to shared owned with full access and the host to shared borrowed. Unsharing requires the reverse shared starting pair, records guest ownership metadata in the host table, and restores the guest to owned with full access. Any other starting pair fails without modification.

Host and hypervisor transitions observed by the self test form a small cycle. Hypervisor owned with host absent donates to host owned with hypervisor absent. Host owned shares to host shared owned with hypervisor shared borrowed, or hands to firmware leaving host shared owned with hypervisor absent. Each share has a matching unshare returning to host owned, duplicate shares and cross shares from a shared state are rejected, and pinning a shared range makes unshare report busy until the pin count drops to zero.

Host and guest transitions support sharing, donation, reclaim and poison. Host owned shares to host shared owned with guest shared borrowed and allows a second guest page with a count of two. Unsharing pages one by one restores host owned when the last share is removed. Donation moves host owned to host absent with guest owned. Guest sharing to host moves to guest shared owned with host shared borrowed. Normal reclaim returns to host owned with guest absent, while forced reclaim returns to host owned with guest poisoned, after which guest share and unshare attempts report a hardware poison failure.

Test expectations record one host state, one hypervisor state and two guest states for two adjacent guest pages. Static self test storage keeps these expectations, a pointer to the backing test page and a pointer to the test virtual CPU. The test guest address is placed in the upper half of the address space based on the configured address width.

The ownership self test is a coverage driver that allocates a single test page, creates a temporary virtual machine, checks initial states across host hypervisor and guest, then invokes each donation share unshare pin reclaim and poison operation asserting both the returned status and the resulting states, and finally destroys the temporary machine and releases the page. A helper combines status assertion with a full state recheck.

Self test machine creation mirrors host address settings into a static machine, prepares its guest stage two tables, distributes supplied pages between the minimum cache reserve and the machine pool based on reference state, reserves a handle and publishes the machine in the global table, returning a static virtual CPU. Destruction removes the published handle while holding the machine table lock.

Two locks serialize shared structures in these fragments. The machine table lock guards insertion and removal of table entries. The hypervisor page directory lock guards private address reservation, hypervisor mapping and large fix block capture.

Hypervisor memory management state includes a global page table object, its directory lock, a bounded array of RAM descriptors with a live count, a base and next pointer allocator for private virtual addresses, per CPU fixmap slots and an optional large block slot. Each fixmap slot pairs a virtual address with a pointer to its leaf table entry.

Fixmap slot capture runs a leaf only walk over one page. It rejects missing entries and entries whose span differs from the level granule, otherwise stores the visited address and entry pointer and then clears the entry while keeping the table page reference elevated so future manual entry changes never need allocation.

Large fix block creation looks for a block aligned RAM window inside the known hypervisor memory descriptors, reserves an aligned private virtual range, maps the RAM there with hypervisor protections and captures the range with the leaf walker under the directory lock. If the compile time feature is disabled the routine reports success without action. Missing RAM windows and reservation or mapping failures are reported as errors.

Fixmap initialization creates one slot per CPU by allocating a private page, mapping a shared hypervisor data page there and capturing the slot, then creates the optional large block. The first failure stops the sequence and is returned to the caller.

Host ownership auditing validates both tracking structures and host stage two entries. RAM claimed by the hypervisor must show hypervisor owned with host absent in tracking and hypervisor owned in the host table, except hypervisor text which may stay host readable when not writable. A leaf walker checks each valid entry page by page, and the public audit walks the combined private and vmemmap quarter starting at the recorded base.

Host page admission for hypervisor use takes the head page from a supplied host cache, performs a host to hypervisor donation to transfer ownership, then removes the page from the cache for hypervisor use. Empty caches and donation races yield no page.

Visible interfaces in these fragments are the host ownership audit, fixmap creation, machine table initialization, ownership self test, self test machine setup and teardown, and the guest to host share and unshare operations. Each is usable from other hypervisor objects in the same dossier.
Machine handle values start at 0x1000, decimal 4096, leaving smaller values reserved.
The reserved machine table entry is the pointer sized sentinel 0xa110ca7ed.

Machine handles index a global table of machine pointers installed once at boot. Initialization asserts at build time that the handle offset plus the maximum protected machine count fits in the handle type and warns if the table was already installed.

The static self test machine and virtual CPU are linked at definition time. The machine memory object points to its own stage two table and architecture block, and the virtual CPU points to that memory object and machine, with its hardware management pointer set to the machine memory object.

Guest memory share and unshare calls first reject unaligned guest addresses without effect. Sharing invokes the guest to host share step and reports success on completion, while a missing guest mapping instead builds a low level write translation fault record with encoded fault address and rewinds the return address by one instruction so the mapping fault is serviced and the call retried via an exit to the host. Unsharing invokes the matching unshare step and reports success only when it completes.

Two pinning hazards appear. Host tables must not use large mappings for uncommon protections because a later page scoped map can split the range and discard ownership state kept only in that entry. Fixmap slots depend on elevated table page references after clearing, so the backing table page must never be freed while the slot exists.

Poisoned guest pages are terminal for sharing and must return a hardware poison error rather than a permission error. Unaligned hypercall addresses must be ignored without table changes. The share retry path must synthesize fault state and rewind correctly, otherwise the guest could skip or repeat the original request.

Remaining globals declare the hypervisor vmemmap base, instruction cache flags, virtual machine identifier width, host vector length limit, a per CPU pointer to the loaded protected virtual CPU, and the branch predictor vector base. Their writers and readers are not visible in these fragments.
